books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.text:
“...That all persons born in the United States and not subject to any foreign power, excluding Indians not taxed, are hereby declared to be citizens of the United States; and such citizens, of every race and color, without regard to any previous condition of slavery or involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall have the same right, in every State and Territory in the United States, to make and enforce contracts, to sue, be parties, and give evidence, to inherit, purchase, lease, sell, hold, and convey real and personal property, and to full and equal benefit of all laws and proceedings for the security of person and property, as is enjoyed by white citizens...”

—Civil Rights Act of 1866, Section 1, April 9, 1866
stimulus.source_note: Civil Rights Act of 1866, Section 1, April 9, 1866. Public domain. Wording verified against the Statutes at Large text (14 Stat. 27) as reproduced by the National Constitution Center. Leading and trailing ellipses mark omitted text.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: President Johnson vetoed this act, and Congress overrode his veto. That override best shows that

options.text: Congress was taking control of Reconstruction policy from the president.
the Supreme Court had ordered Congress to pass the act.
options.misconception: Background: the Court played no part here; this was a fight between Congress and the president.

options.text: Southern states had asked for federal protection.
options.misconception: Background: Southern states opposed the act and the Congress that passed it.

options.text: the Freedmen’s Bureau had closed its offices.
options.misconception: Background: the Bureau was still running in 1866, and Congress had just voted to extend it.

rationales.A: Johnson had run Reconstruction on his own while Congress was out of session, pardoning Confederates and accepting their governments. By overriding his veto, Congress announced that it, not the president, would set the terms.
rationales.B: Background: the Court played no part here; this was a fight between Congress and the president.
rationales.C: Background: Southern states opposed the act and the Congress that passed it.
rationales.D: Background: the Bureau was still running in 1866, and Congress had just voted to extend it.
rationales.general:
1. A veto override needs two thirds of both houses, so it is never routine.
2. Background: Johnson had spent a year rebuilding the South on lenient terms while Congress was away.
3. Overriding him on this act, and on the Freedmen’s Bureau bill, moved the steering wheel to Congress.
4. From here on, Reconstruction would be Congress’s program.
Remember: a veto override is a power shift, not just a disagreement.
